title: Dark and Lovely
sum: The Song begins with a title and then, without warning, a woman's voice. She wants kisses. She wants her lover near. She says the young women love his name, calls herself dark and lovely, and explains that her brothers made her guard their vineyards while her own went unguarded. She asks him where he pastures his flock, is answered by a teasing voice, and the two begin to praise each other under a roof of cedar and cypress.

God is not named in the chapter. The reader is dropped into a love already under way, and learns how to listen: the voices change without labels, and 'I', 'you', 'he' and 'we' have to be told apart by the Hebrew's gender and number. The Plain English Translation adds no speaker names inside the verses; the cards below show who is likely speaking.
readings: Read as love poetry

A woman speaks of her lover to the other young women, to him, and to her brothers' world. The images (oil, wine, a king's rooms, a mare among stallions, a bag of myrrh between her breasts) all draw their strength from the body and from the scents of gardens. This is the reading of most scholars today (Fox, Exum, Murphy, Longman, Garrett, Bloch).
Read as the story of God and Israel

Rabbinic readers took the king as God and the woman as Israel. In the Targum the opening kiss is God's giving of the Torah, and in Song of Songs Rabbah 'black' and 'lovely' are read of Israel's sin and Israel's merit.
Read as the soul and Christ

From Origen on, Christian readers heard the soul or the Church asking to be kissed by the Word, and 'dark and lovely' as the sinner made beautiful by grace. Bernard of Clairvaux's early sermons on the Song linger long on 'Let him kiss me'.

views.H: The title ties the poem to Solomon, but in the text the chief figure is a country woman with brothers and a mother's house. The mention of Kedar and of royal tent cloth suggests a speaker who knows desert and palace alike. The place names so far run from En-gedi to Kedar to Egypt.
views.L: The chapter matches the openings of Egyptian love songs, where a girl speaks of her lover to her friends and then to him. Fox finds in those songs the same use of 'sister', 'brother' and 'my darling' and the same images of wine, oil and plants.
views.J: The rabbis made 1:1 a seal of holiness: the Song is Solomon's, and the name Shelomoh was read as 'the King to whom peace (shalom) belongs', God. The Targum retells the Song as the history of God and Israel from the Exodus on, and Rashi reads it as Israel's love for God in exile.
views.X: Origen's commentary and Bernard's sermons make 1:2 the Church's cry for the Word to come, and 1:5 the dark soul made lovely. The Fathers took the 'daughters of Jerusalem' as souls still learning and the brothers as the Church's enemies. Later Protestant preachers read 'dark and lovely' of the believer, justified and still a sinner.
views.M: The woman is the first speaker and she opens the book by naming her own wish. Trible and Exum note that she speaks first, longest and with the most freedom. Her dark skin is stated without apology. Her brothers' control (1:6) puts the question whether she is free to love, which later chapters answer.

deep.b:
The Hebrew marks speakers by grammar: feminine singular for the woman, masculine singular for the man, plural for groups. It gives no names. In chapter 1 the woman speaks in 1:2–7, to him, to the daughters, and to him again. Scholars assign 1:8 differently (the daughters, the man, or the woman's own thought) and 1:9–11 too (the man, or the chorus joined to him). The reader should expect the voice to turn without notice, as in a spoken poem.

The Plain English Translation adds no labels inside the verses. The headings name the unit and the cards give the likely voices.

The woman explains that the sun has looked at her and that her brothers sent her into the vineyards (1:6). That is why her skin is darker than that of the 'daughters of Jerusalem', who stay indoors. The Hebrew gives no sign of a different people. Origen heard the dark bride as the Ethiopian wife of Moses (Numbers 12:1) and as the Queen of Sheba, which the text does not say. Today the line is read as a statement about class and labor and also about beauty, which cannot be ranked by color.

The Plain English Translation is made from the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex, with the Aleppo Codex and the Ketiv and Qere markers as given in the word list. The Septuagint is quoted from Swete's printing of Codex Vaticanus, and a reading that only that codex shows is named by the codex. The Dead Sea Scrolls are read in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription: 6Q6 preserves parts of 1:1 to 1:7, and 4QCant-a, 4QCant-b and 4QCant-c preserve parts of chapters 2 to 7. The Targum is cited from Philip Alexander's translation (The Aramaic Bible 17A) and the Latin Vulgate from the Weber–Gryson edition. Where the Plain English Translation follows a reading other than the Masoretic text, the variants say so.

echoes: Proverbs 7:17–18; Isaiah 5:1–7; 1 Kings 4:32; 1 Kings 10:28–29; Genesis 25:13; Psalm 45:8; 1 Samuel 24:1; John 12:3

settings.what: The title
settings.by: The editor or collector of the Song
settings.when: when the poems were gathered under Solomon's name
settings.why: The title names the book as the best of songs and ties it to Solomon, the king who 1 Kings 4:32 says wrote 1,005 songs. Whether that means 'by', 'for' or 'in the manner of' is debated.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers the title was a claim to royal wisdom and Israel's golden age, which helped the Song be kept and read.
views: Jewish and Christian tradition for most of history: Solomon wrote it, as 1 Kings 4:32 would lead one to expect.
Many scholars: the name is a literary tribute, and the poems come from various hands.
Some take the preposition as 'for' or 'about': a collection made for a king's wedding.

settings.what: First cycle of longing and praise
settings.by: The woman, mostly; the man; the daughters of Jerusalem; her brothers (reported)
settings.to: The woman to her lover and to the daughters of Jerusalem; the man to her
settings.when: in the poem's world, a time of early love and waiting, with no clear count of days
settings.why: To show a love in its first heat: longing in his absence, praise when he is near, and a plea to the daughters not to hurry love (2:7). It sets the tone and many images for the book.
settings.readers: At a wedding feast the poems give the guests and the couple a language of praise. In a scribal school they were a classic of love poetry. In the temple community they were read as love between God and Israel.
views: The poems are songs for a wedding festival (Wetzstein's Syrian parallels), where the couple are king and queen.
Separate songs gathered by Jerusalem scribes of the Persian or Greek age (Fox counts 31 poems).
The Targum and the rabbis hear a dialogue between God and his people.

settings.what: The answer to the woman's question
settings.by: Debated: the daughters of Jerusalem, her lover, or the woman herself
settings.when: as she asks where he pastures his flock
settings.why: To answer her question in 1:7 with a tease or a direction: if you do not know, follow the tracks of the flock. Who speaks decides whether it is her friends teasing, her lover playing a shepherd, or her own second thought.
settings.readers: Hearers who knew shepherds' camps would hear a playful riddle, the kind of exchange that fills courtship songs.
views: The women answer her, teasing: look among the shepherds' tents (Murphy, Exum).
He answers as the shepherd she is looking for.
She answers herself in the voice of her friends.
The Church or God tells the soul to follow the footsteps of the saints.

settings.what: The first praise from him
settings.by: The man; in 1:11 'we' may be him with his friends, or the daughters speaking for him
settings.when: as he answers her search
settings.why: To answer her longing with praise: a mare among Pharaoh's chariots, cheeks and neck set with jewels, and a promise of gold ornaments with silver dots. The plural of 1:11 leaves open who promises the gift.
settings.readers: Hearers would take the jewelry as the gifts of a wedding, and the mare as a bold praise of a woman who stirs everyone around her.
views: He speaks with a plural of generosity or royalty (Fox).
'We' is the lover with his companions, as the chorus speaks for her in 1:4 (Garrett).
The chorus sings the promise on his behalf.

settings.what: The woman's self-description
settings.by: The woman
settings.when: as they stare at her
settings.why: She tells the other women not to stare at her sun-darkened skin and explains it: her brothers set her to work and she could not tend her own vineyard. It names her pride and her loss.
settings.readers: Readers who knew field labor and family control would hear a young woman defending her worth.
views: The line is about class: a field worker, not a lady (Fox, Bloch).
Some hear a woman of dark complexion from another land (compare Kedar), but the text says the sun made her dark.
The soul stained by sin and made lovely by grace (Origen, Bernard).

title: Spring, and the Little Foxes
sum: The woman praises her lover as an apple tree among the trees of the woods and says she is a spring crocus. He brings her into the banquet house and love is his banner over her. Lovesick, she asks for raisin cakes and apples and for his arm. She makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear not to wake love until it wants to be awake, the first of the book's three oaths.

Then she hears him coming over the hills like a gazelle. He stands at the wall and calls her out into the spring: the winter is over, the vines are in bloom. The chapter ends with the small foxes among the vines and with a request that he turn back, like a gazelle on the mountains, until the day breathes.
readings: Read as love poetry

A courtship scene. She speaks and he answers in his own voice, quoted by her (2:10–14). The images of fruit, shade, wine and flowers are all pictures of pleasure, and the spring is the season of love in the poetry of many peoples. This is the most widely held reading today (Fox, Murphy, Exum).
Read as the history of Israel

In the Targum and in Song of Songs Rabbah, the lover who leaps over the mountains is God coming to redeem Israel from Egypt in the spring; the winter is the bondage, the voice of the dove is the voice of the Torah, and the foxes are enemies.
Read as the soul's progress

Origen, Gregory of Nyssa and Bernard read the chapter as stages of the soul's growth: the first taste, the banquet house of teaching, the vision of the lover who looks through the lattice, and the call to leave the winter of sin. The foxes are heresies or small vices.

views.H: The chapter's flowers and fruits fit the spring in the hills of Judah and the Sharon plain. The mention of vineyards in bloom fixes the season at about March or April, the time of Passover, and later Jewish practice made that the time to read the Song.
views.L: Fox compares the call to come out into the spring with Egyptian songs where a young man waits at the house. In the Cairo Love Songs and the Chester Beatty papyri a girl longs to see her 'brother' and he stands at her wall. Theocritus has a lover at a door. The sickness of love and the apple tree are old motifs.
views.J: The rabbis read the whole chapter as the Exodus: the voice of the beloved is God at Sinai, the wall is Egypt, the winter is the long bondage, and the little foxes are Israel's enemies. Rashi reads 2:7 as an oath Israel took not to rebel against the nations or to force the end of exile.
views.X: The apple tree is Christ whose shade shelters the Church (Origen, Ambrose, Bernard). The banquet house is the Church or the Eucharist, the banner is love (compare John 13:34–35), the foxes are heretics (Origen, Augustine). Later preachers took 2:1 as Christ's own words, which the Hebrew does not support.
views.M: The woman is the one who goes to the banquet, asks for food and an embrace, and gives the oath. Trible sees in 2:10–14 a garden image that reverses Eden: the woman is invited out, not driven out. Exum notes that his words are all quoted by her, so he speaks only as she hears him.

deep.b: The chapter is full of spring: the winter rains are over, blossoms are out, the vines are in flower and the doves are cooing. Israel's Passover falls in this season, and the Jewish custom of reading the Song at Passover rests on that fit as well as on the allegory of the Exodus. Song of Songs Rabbah ties each phrase of 2:8–14 to the Exodus. The custom of reading the Song at Passover is first described in the minor tractate Soferim (chapter 14), usually dated to about the eighth century; the rabbinic reading itself is earlier.

deep.h: The little foxes in five readings
deep.b: The verse about the foxes is one of the most debated in the book. The Hebrew says only 'seize for us foxes, small foxes, which ruin vineyards', 'for our vineyards are in bloom'. Real foxes eat grapes (Nehemiah 4:3; Lamentations 5:18), so the plainest reading is a vineyard song, which might be a work song or a children's riddle. In a book where the vineyard is the woman (1:6; 8:12), the foxes are whatever spoils young love: rivals, rough suitors, brothers, or her own fears. Origen and Augustine read them as heretics; Bernard as small faults that eat away at the soul. See the note at 2:15.

deep.title: 'Go for yourself' in 2:10 and Genesis 12:1
deep.b: The invitation 'lekhi lakh' (2:10, 13) is the feminine form of God's call to Abram, 'lekh lekha' (Genesis 12:1). I suggest the Song may be using the language of a call to leave home: she is called out of her mother's house toward a new place, as Abram was. The Song's repeated references to a mother's house (3:4; 8:2) make a departure from it a theme. I have not seen this proposed in the commentaries; the sound is the same in Hebrew, but the connection may be accidental.
deep.refs: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 22:2; Song of Songs 2:10; Song of Songs 2:13; Song of Songs 3:4; Song of Songs 8:2

echoes: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 3:8; Isaiah 35:1; Hosea 3:1; 2 Samuel 6:19; Nehemiah 4:3; Exodus 12:1–14; Exodus 33:22

settings.what: The spring invitation and the night search (2:8–3:5)
settings.by: The woman, who quotes the man's invitation (2:10–14), then speaks alone
settings.to: The woman to herself and to the daughters of Jerusalem; the man (quoted) to her
settings.when: in spring, as the lover comes to her wall; then at night, in the city
settings.why: To show love as a visit that comes and goes: the lover arrives with the spring, calls her out, and leaves; she searches the city for him and finds him (3:1–4). It teaches the daughters, who are charged again at 3:5, that love cannot be forced.
settings.readers: At a wedding, the invitation to leave the house for the spring fields would be sung by the groom's party. Readers in the temple community took the whole as God coming to Israel.
views: Girl and boy, the family house and the fields; a young woman in a town and a lover who visits (Exum, Fox).
The night search of chapter 3 is a dream or fantasy that follows the day's visit (Murphy, Bloch).
God coming to Egypt, leaping over obstacles (Song of Songs Rabbah; Targum).

settings.what: The oath to the daughters of Jerusalem (2:7; 3:5; 8:4)
settings.by: The woman
settings.when: at the close of each of the book's first three cycles
settings.why: To charge the daughters, in the form of an oath, not to wake or stir love until it wants to. The same words stand at 2:7 and 3:5, and again at 8:4 without the gazelles and does. What she is asking of them is the Song's most debated question.
settings.readers: For hearers at a wedding or in a school, the oath was the refrain that told them how to take the love they heard: not to be hurried, not to be disturbed, not to be forced.
views: A warning to the young about haste before the time (Garrett).
A request not to break in on lovers in each other's arms (Fox).
Love cannot be made to come by drugs, magic or pressure.
God makes Israel swear not to rebel against the nations or force the end of exile (Song of Songs Rabbah; Babylonian Talmud, Ketubbot 111a).
Christian writers took it as a charge to leave the Bridegroom's rest undisturbed.

settings.what: The foxes in the vineyards
settings.by: Debated: the man, the woman, her brothers, or the daughters
settings.to: Debated: the other lovers' group, or the brothers
settings.when: as the vineyards flower
settings.why: A request or a riddle to catch the foxes that spoil the flowering vines. Because the vineyard is the woman's image in 1:6 and 8:12, the line is a warning that something could harm love when it is ready to bloom.
settings.readers: Hearers who knew vineyards would see a real task; those who had read the earlier lines would hear a warning.
views: The brothers guard the family vineyard and the girl (compare 1:6; 8:8–9). Murphy and others.
Quoted by the woman as a playful reply to his invitation (Fox, Garrett).
Origen, Augustine and Bernard: the foxes are heretics or vices.

title: The Night Search and Solomon's Litter
sum: Alone on her bed night after night, the woman looks for the one she loves with her whole self, and does not find him. She gets up and goes through the city, is found by the watchmen, and asks them if they have seen him. She has hardly passed them when she finds him, holds him, and takes him to her mother's house. Then she makes the daughters of Jerusalem swear, once more, not to wake love before it wants to be awake.

Without a break the poem turns to a procession: smoke rising from the wilderness, Solomon's bed carried on poles and ringed by sixty armed men, its silver posts and purple seat made by the daughters of Jerusalem. The daughters of Zion are told to come out and look at the king on his wedding day. The scene has moved from a woman in the dark to a king in the light, and the reader must decide how the two fit.
readings: Read as dream and procession

A woman's night dream is followed by a wedding parade, two scenes of the same love: one private and anxious, one public and splendid. The royal litter is the poem's picture of the wedding (Fox, Murphy).
Read as the history of Israel

The Targum tells the story of Israel from the Exodus on: the smoke is the cloud of glory over Israel in the wilderness, the litter is the Tabernacle, and the wedding day is Sinai (Mishnah Taanit 4:8). Song of Songs Rabbah counts the sixty warriors as the sixty letters of the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) or the sixty myriads of Israel.
Read as the Church and Christ

The search at night is the soul or the Church seeking Christ (Hippolytus, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa). The litter is the Church or the cross, the warriors are the angels or the teachers, and the crown is the crown of thorns or the Church's crown.

views.H: The litter, with Lebanon cedar and silver, gold and purple, stands for the luxury of Solomon's court, and the word apiryon is one of the few words that scholars use to argue a date. The sixty warriors echo David's mighty men. The wedding day is Solomon's, but the poem may use a king's wedding as the model for any couple's.
views.L: The two scenes match a common pairing in love poetry: private longing and public celebration. Egyptian love songs include a girl who searches for her love, and wedding songs that treat the groom as a king. In Wetzstein's account of Syrian weddings, the groom was carried in procession as king in a decorated chair.
views.J: The rabbis read 3:11 as a verse on Sinai and the Temple (Mishnah Taanit 4:8). The Targum retells all of 3:6–11 as the Exodus: the pillar of cloud and smoke, the Tabernacle, the priests, the Law. Rashi follows this, and sees the daughters of Zion as Israel.
views.X: Hippolytus links the woman's search to Mary Magdalene seeking the Lord at the tomb, and Origen to the soul's quest for the Word. Gregory of Nyssa reads the endless search as the nature of the soul's life with God. The litter of Solomon is the Church for Ambrose and Bernard, and the crown his mother gave him is the flesh he took from Mary.
views.M: Her search is brave and unprotected, and she finds him by her own effort. Exum asks whether the second half belongs to a different voice: the king is silent here and the daughters are told what to see. Some readers contrast the woman at large in the city with the guarded king.

deep.h: The two parts of the chapter
deep.b: The chapter has two scenes with no sign of a join. 3:1–5 is a first-person story by the woman. 3:6–11 is a description by a group of onlookers, who ask who is coming (3:6), describe a litter (3:7–10), and call the daughters of Zion to look (3:11). Some readers hold that the second part is another poem; others see the sequence as one wedding: after the bride has found him, the cortege comes. Both readings are given in the notes.

Solomon appears here as a figure of splendor: his bed, his litter, his crown. He is named seven times in the book, and the way he is seen changes. In the title he is the book's patron (1:1). In 1:5 his tent curtains are a mark of beauty. In 3:7–11 he is the groom. In 8:11–12 he is the owner of a rich vineyard whose thousand silver pieces the woman refuses to want. It is possible that the poem uses him as a stock figure of royal love, and the woman's own lover, the shepherd, as a contrast. The notes list the views.

echoes: Genesis 24:28; Genesis 24:67; Jeremiah 29:13; Hosea 5:6; Psalm 91:5; 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 10:2; 2 Samuel 23:8; John 20:1; John 20:11–18

settings.what: The wedding: litter, praise and the garden (3:6–5:1)
settings.by: Unnamed onlookers (3:6–11); the man (4:1–5:1); the woman (4:16); an unnamed voice (5:1c)
settings.to: The daughters of Zion (3:11); the woman (4:1–5:1); 'friends' (5:1c)
settings.when: on the wedding day, in the poem's world
settings.why: To bring love to its fulfilment in a public and a private scene: the cortege of the king, the praise of the bride from head to breast, the invitation 'my sister, my bride', the locked garden opened and the voice that blesses it. It is the center of the book.
settings.readers: At a wedding feast these lines would be sung by the guests and the groom's party. For the scribal school, a showpiece of praise. For the temple community, the wedding of God and Israel.
views: Wetzstein's Syrian wedding songs, with the groom as king and the praise of the bride as the main song.
A song for a king's wedding, like Psalm 45.
The Targum reads the whole unit as Sinai, the Tabernacle and the covenant.

settings.what: The litter of Solomon
settings.by: Unnamed voices of onlookers; the last verse calls the daughters of Zion
settings.when: as the wedding procession approaches from the wilderness
settings.why: To describe a cortege, with a cloud of scent and a litter ringed by sixty armed men, and to invite the daughters to come out and see the king on his wedding day.
settings.readers: The first readers heard a famous scene of royal splendor, set in Solomon's day, and perhaps recognized in it the pattern of their own weddings.
views: The coming figure is the bride (Murphy, Garrett).
The litter and the king are the subject (Fox).
The Targum: Israel coming up with the cloud and the Tabernacle.

title: My Sister, My Bride
sum: The man looks at his bride and praises her from her hair to her breasts: eyes like doves behind her veil, hair like a flock of goats streaming down a hill, teeth like shorn sheep come up from the wash, lips like a scarlet thread, a neck like a tower hung with shields, breasts like twin fawns. He ends, 'All of you is beautiful, my darling, and you have no blemish.'

Then he calls her 'my sister, my bride' down from the mountains of Lebanon, tells her she has stolen his heart with one of her eyes, and says her lovemaking is better than wine and her scents better than any spice. She is a garden locked and a spring sealed, a park of pomegranates and every spice, a well of living water. She answers by calling the north wind and the south wind to blow on her garden, and she asks him to come in.
readings: Read as a wedding song

The first full praise of the bride, in the form of the Arabic wasf, sung by the groom on or after the wedding. The garden is the bride, the unlocking is the consummation, and the chapter ends with her invitation (Delitzsch, Fox, Murphy).
Read as the love of God and Israel
The Targum retells 4:1–15 as praise of Israel and its leaders: its judges and priests, and Moses and Aaron as the twin fawns; the garden is Israel, kept for God and sealed by the Law.
Read as Christ and the Church (or the soul)

The wasf is the praise of the Church, whom Christ makes without blemish (Ephesians 5:27); the locked garden is the Church or Mary; the winds are the Spirit; the invitation of 4:16 is the Church's prayer that Christ come to her.

views.H: The place names (Lebanon, Amana, Senir, Hermon) lie to the north, and the garden is made of imported spices. The Persian word pardes (4:13) is one of the Song's late words, and the wasf form is old, known in Egypt and in Arabic wedding songs. The tower of David and the shields point toward Jerusalem's armories.
views.L: The wasf fits a long tradition of praise-songs for a bride. Nothing in Egyptian love songs is exactly like it, but Egyptian songs have 'sister' and 'brother' and a girl compared to plants and birds. Syrian wedding songs recorded by Wetzstein in the 1800s praise the bride limb by limb during the 'king's week'.
views.J: In the Targum the praise of 4:1–5 becomes the praise of Israel's leaders and institutions, and Moses and Aaron stand for the twin fawns. The 'locked garden' of 4:12 was read as Israel kept holy for God. Medieval commentators such as Rashi also read the garden as Israel.
views.X: Ambrose, Jerome and other Latin writers call Mary the enclosed garden and the sealed fountain, and the liturgy gives her 4:7 ('all fair'). Gregory of Nyssa and Bernard use the bride's praise for the soul. Protestant interpreters from the seventeenth century read the garden as the believer or the Church opened to Christ.
views.M: The man praises her; she alone opens the garden. Trible reads the garden as Eden returned and the woman as free to give. Some feminist readers warn that the wasf looks at her body from outside, and note that she in turn makes a wasf of him (5:10–16).

deep.b:
A wasf is a descriptive praise of the body. The Song has four, and each has its own shape. The first (this one, 4:1–7) runs from the head downward (hair, eyes, teeth, lips, cheek, neck, breasts), then sums up (4:7). The woman's praise of him in 5:10–16 also runs downward; the third, 6:4–10, is shorter and repeats parts of the first; the fourth, in 7:1–9, runs from the feet upward. The comparisons are never meant to be drawn. They tell how the lover feels, and many draw on city and countryside at once (a tower, a flock, a fruit).

Egyptian love songs and the Arabic wasf-songs of Syrian weddings, recorded by Wetzstein and used by Delitzsch, give the nearest parallels. The Plain English Translation translates the body parts with plain words; the notes explain the images.

The locked garden and the sealed spring (4:12–15) recall the first garden of Genesis 2:8–15, with its river and its trees, and the garden of 5:1 has the same fruit-eating, drinking and sleeping. Phyllis Trible argued that the Song reverses the failure of Eden: the man and woman delight in each other and are not ashamed. In Genesis 3:8 the man and woman hear the LORD walking in the garden 'in the breezy part of the day', and the Song's 'until the day breathes' (2:17; 4:6) echoes that breeze. See the note at 7:10 for the larger argument.

deep.title: The winds that wake the garden
deep.b: The woman asks the north and south winds to 'wake' her garden, using the same verb as the oath (2:7; 3:5; 8:4: do not wake love until it wants). I suggest this is the Song's way of showing that the oath was not a ban on desire but a condition on its timing: once the garden is ready, waking is what she asks for. Commentators often note the repeated verb; I have not seen this reading of it argued in the commentaries on the oath, though it may overlap with remarks about love 'waking' in its own time.
deep.refs: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 3:5; Song of Songs 4:16; Song of Songs 8:4

echoes: Genesis 2:8–15; Genesis 3:8; Exodus 3:8; Exodus 30:23; Proverbs 5:3; Proverbs 5:15–18; Proverbs 7:17; Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:10–14; Ephesians 5:27; Isaiah 47:2

settings.what: The first praise of the bride
settings.by: The man
settings.when: as the wedding day moves toward night, in the poem's world
settings.why: To praise her from the head down, so that she knows how she looks to him and how much he is moved. The praise ends with 'no blemish', which gives her complete acceptance.
settings.readers: At a wedding feast the guests would sing or hear such a praise of the bride; in the school, it was a model of the wasf. The temple community took it as God's praise of Israel.
views: A praise sung for the bride at her wedding (Wetzstein, Delitzsch).
A set piece in a book of love poems (Fox).
The Targum's praise of Israel's sages, priests and Temple.

settings.what: The garden opened
settings.by: The woman (4:16); the man (5:1a–b); an unnamed voice (5:1c, 'Eat, friends, drink')
settings.to: The winds and the lover (4:16); the bride (5:1a–b); the friends (5:1c)
settings.when: on the night of the wedding, in the poem's world
settings.why: To bring the wedding to its high point: she opens the garden, he enters and takes, and a voice blesses them. The call to the friends to eat and drink is the only line that is not from the lovers.
settings.readers: The voice of 5:1c would be the wedding guests or the groom's friends; the scene reads like the fulfilment of the feast.
views: The woman, the man and the chorus
Most readers: 5:1c is the friends (Fox, Garrett).
Some Jewish and Christian readers: the divine voice blesses the union (Rashi's Israel; Christ and the Church).
Some take the whole of 5:1 as his words, calling all to join the feast (Murphy).

The Church's liturgy uses lines of the Song for Mary: 'You are all fair' (4:7) on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, 'Who is this?' (3:6; 8:5) and 'Arise, my darling' (2:10) for the Assumption, and the enclosed garden and sealed spring (4:12) as titles. This is a spiritual or accommodated use of the text, built on the Church's reading of Mary as the first of the redeemed; it does not replace the Song's sense as love between Christ and the Church or as married love.

Eastern hymns call Mary 'Bride unwedded' (the Akathist Hymn), but the Song itself is read first as the bride (the soul or the Church) and her Bridegroom, Christ. The Marian use belongs to the Church's praise and not to a strict reading of the text.

Lutherans honor Mary as the Mother of God but do not apply the Song to her; they read it as God's gift of marriage or of Christ and the Church (Luther's lectures read it as a praise of good government).

The Reformed churches do not apply the Song to Mary; their reading is of Christ and the believer, or of married love. Their confessions direct worship to God alone and not to saints or angels (Westminster Confession 21.2), so Marian teaching is not built on it.

Anglicans differ among themselves. The Thirty-Nine Articles (Article 22) reject the invoking of saints, and many Anglicans, like the Reformed, do not read the Song of Mary; Anglo-Catholic parishes keep the Marian feasts and their texts. Anglican and Roman Catholic theologians have also studied Mary together (ARCIC, 2005).

title: The Knock at the Door
sum: The wedding feast ends with a voice telling the friends to eat, drink and be drunk (5:1). Then the scene breaks. The woman is asleep, but her heart is awake, and she hears her lover knocking: his hair is wet with the night. She answers that she has taken off her tunic and washed her feet. He puts his hand through the opening, and her insides churn. She gets up, with myrrh dripping from her hands onto the bolt, and opens. He is gone.

She searches the city, and the watchmen beat her and take her shawl. She charges the daughters of Jerusalem: if you find him, tell him love has made me sick. They ask her what is so special about him, and she answers with a head-to-foot praise of her lover in gold, ivory and marble, ending 'this is my lover, and this is my friend.'
readings: Read as dream
A woman's anxiety dream about hesitating too long: the knock, the delay, the vanished lover, the beating. The dream has the mix of desire and fear that waking life hides (Murphy, Bloch).
Read as the story of God and Israel
In Song of Songs Rabbah God knocks at Israel's door in exile, asking an opening as small as a needle's eye; Israel is slow, and God withdraws his presence; yet she still seeks and praises him.
Read as the soul and Christ

The soul resting in the world hears Christ at the door (compare Revelation 3:20), delays, and finds him gone; she must seek again and is wounded by those who should guard her. The praise of him is the soul's love for Christ (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Bernard).

views.H: The details (a door with a latch hole, a wall with watchmen, a woman's shawl) fit the walled towns of Judah. The materials in the man's praise (gold, ivory, lapis, marble) are the imports of Solomon's days (1 Kings 10:18, 22), though the praise may use them as symbols and not as a record.
views.L: The knock at the door is an old motif of love poetry in many cultures. Egyptian love songs include a lover at the girl's closed door, and Greek and Latin poetry has the 'paraklausithyron' (the lover's song at a shut door); the Song reverses it by making the woman the one inside, and the one who comes out to search.
views.J: The midrash has God say 'open to me' (Song of Songs Rabbah 5:2) and Israel's slowness cause his departure. The beating by the watchmen is the persecution of Israel by the nations. The praise of the beloved (5:10–16) was used by the Kabbalists as a description of God, the basis of the mystical 'Shi'ur Qomah' tradition that measures God's body; many later Jewish thinkers rejected a literal reading of it.
views.X: Origen and Gregory of Nyssa find in the second search the desertion of the soul, who must go on seeking: Gregory sees the wounds as a stage of the soul's growth. Bernard's sermons stop at 3:1, so this chapter was taken up by his continuers, such as Gilbert of Hoyland. The praise of the lover is the praise of Christ in his body and church, from the head (gold) to the legs (pillars of marble).
views.M: The woman is both bold and punished. Trible and Exum read 5:7 as an honest picture of the risk a woman runs when she acts on her desire in public. The man's absence is her fault only if the poem says so, and it does not. Some readers note that the daughters are not her rivals but her helpers.

deep.h: Real or dream? Two night searches
deep.b: The two night scenes mirror each other. In 3:1–5 she searches, finds him, and takes him to her mother's room. In 5:2–8 he comes to her, she delays, he is gone, and she is beaten. Scholars read the pair as one dream and one story, as two dreams, or as a deliberate contrast: the first search ends in joy because it ends in her mother's house; the second shows love's cost. The poem does not say whether either happened. The Plain English Translation adds nothing to tell the reader.

5:4 says the lover 'sent his hand in through the opening', and her insides churned. The Hebrew words are ordinary words for a hand and a hole, and many scholars hear a second, sexual sense in them (see Isaiah 57:8 for yad). The Song uses double meaning throughout: gardens, fruit, doors and keys work on two levels. The Plain English Translation gives the plain meaning and the note explains the second. A young reader can take the passage at the first level, and an older one at both.

echoes: Revelation 3:20; Ruth 3:4; Isaiah 3:23; Isaiah 57:8; Jeremiah 31:20; Exodus 30:23; Exodus 28:20; Proverbs 17:17; Daniel 2:32

settings.what: The knock, the second night search and the praise of the lover (5:2–6:3)
settings.by: The woman, who quotes the man (5:2) and the daughters (5:9); the daughters of Jerusalem (5:9; 6:1)
settings.to: The daughters of Jerusalem; her lover
settings.when: at night, then on the next day, in the poem's world; or in a dream
settings.why: To show the cost and the strength of desire: she delays, loses him, is beaten, and still praises him. The question of the daughters (5:9) draws out the praise that tells who he is. At the end she finds where he is: gone down to his garden (6:2).
settings.readers: Hearers who knew their cities' night patrols would feel the danger. The woman's praise of her lover's body (5:10–16) answers the man's praise of hers in 4:1–7.
views: A long night's dream of delay and loss (Murphy, Bloch).
A real night in the poem's world, told by the woman (Exum).
God knocks and withdraws; Israel seeks him and praises him (Song of Songs Rabbah).

settings.what: The woman's praise of her lover
settings.by: The woman (answering the daughters of Jerusalem)
settings.when: the day after the second search, as the daughters offer to help
settings.why: The daughters ask what makes her lover better than another. She answers with the second wasf, from head to legs, so they will know whom to look for and why she is sick with love.
settings.readers: A group of women hearing another woman describe a man; the poem lets the woman's gaze fall on him, as his fell on her in 4:1–7.
views: A praise of the groom, like the praise of the bride (Fox).
The Kabbalistic Shi'ur Qomah reads it as God's glory; Origen as Christ.
A description in the manner of a cult statue (Pope).

title: Tirzah, Jerusalem and the Dance
sum: The daughters of Jerusalem offer to help look for the lost lover, and the woman answers at once: he has gone down to his garden, to graze among the lilies. 'I belong to my lover and my lover belongs to me.' The man's voice returns with praise: 'You are beautiful, my darling, like Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, fearsome as troops with banners.' He asks her to turn her eyes away, because they overpower him, and repeats the praise of her hair, teeth and face.

He sets her against sixty queens and eighty concubines and countless young women: one is his dove. The women who see her call her happy. A voice asks who this is who looks down like the dawn, as lovely as the moon, as clear as the sun. A garden scene follows, with the obscure verse 6:12, and the chapter ends with the cry 'Come back, Shulammite!' and the question about the dance of the two camps.
readings: Read as love poetry

The man praises her again and chooses her over a royal harem; the daughters and the crowd call her blessed; the final scene is a dance. The images of dawn, moon and sun, with the armies and banners, make her a figure of dazzling power (Fox, Murphy, Garrett).
Read as the story of God and Israel
The Targum reads 6:8–10 as God choosing Israel from all the nations and kings, who bless her, and 6:13 as the call to Israel to return to the Law. The 'two camps' are Israel and the angels.
Read as the Church and the soul

Cyprian and later writers read 6:9 as the unity of the one Church; the sun, moon and dawn as the Church's light from Christ (Origen, Ambrose). Others read the garden of nuts as the soul's inner life, and the Shulammite as the soul called to return and be seen.

views.H: Tirzah, an old northern capital, set beside Jerusalem is one of the clues scholars use for dating (see the opening pages). The harem numbers do not match Solomon's, which is a clue that the king is not meant to be Solomon, or that the numbers are a formula. 'Mahanaim' and 'Shulammite' tie the chapter to Gilead and the Jezreel valley.
views.L: The numbers 'sixty, eighty, and countless' are a formula known from wisdom writing. The three lights, and 'fearsome as armies', echo Mesopotamian praise of the goddess Ishtar (Keel). Egyptian love songs also place the one girl above all others, as the 'one without equal'.
views.J: The midrash and the Targum read 6:9 as Israel the one chosen nation; 6:10 as Israel's rise from exile like the dawn; 6:13 as the call to return (teshuvah). The Shulammite is Israel, 'complete' (shalem) with the Law, or the land called to peace.
views.X: Cyprian reads 'one is my dove' as the Church. Ambrose, Jerome and Bernard use 6:10 for the Church shining with the light of Christ, and the Catholic liturgy uses it for Mary. The Shulammite in some Latin writers is the soul 'made perfect' or the Church 'at peace'.
views.M: The woman is chosen not by number but by name, and not for royal rank: she is 'my dove'. Others praise her. Her eyes overpower him, which is a power, not weakness. Exum and Trible stress that she is seen, and the crowd's wish to 'look' (6:13) raises the question whose gaze rules.

deep.b: The name hashulammit occurs only in 6:13 (twice). The best-supported view is a woman from Shunem, a town near the hill of Moreh in the Jezreel valley. Two women of Shunem appear in the Bible: Abishag, who was brought to warm David in his old age (1 Kings 1:3), and the rich woman who housed Elisha (2 Kings 4). Some commentators, and a long line of readers, have made the Song's heroine Abishag and the lover Solomon or a shepherd. The text does not say. Others read Shulammit as the feminine of Shelomoh, 'Solomon': 'the Solomoness', which would make her his mate, a kind of royal queen in a love song. All of these are views.

The praise of 6:4–7 repeats 4:1–3 almost line for line. The repetition is one of the signals that the Song may be built from a limited stock of lines, reused by different singers. Fox sees an anthology. Others, such as Garrett and Exum, see the second praise as a change: she has become more than an object of his gaze, and the praise now ends with her dominion over him (6:5) and the crowd's praise (6:9).

deep.title: Tirzah and Jerusalem as the two halves of one land
deep.b: It is already published that naming Tirzah beside Jerusalem may point to an early date or a northern setting. My own suggestion is a different one, that the pair also works as a picture: the north's capital and the south's capital together, as one woman. If so, the verse imagines the people before the split of Solomon's kingdom, whole and not divided, as the beloved who is chosen from among the nations. I cannot show this from the text; it is a guess that fits the stress on 'one' in 6:9. It overlaps loosely with the Targum's reading of the verse as the whole of Israel.
deep.refs: 1 Kings 12:16–20; 1 Kings 14:17; Song of Songs 6:4; Song of Songs 6:9; Hosea 2:14–20

echoes: 1 Kings 1:3; 1 Kings 11:3; 1 Kings 14:17; 1 Kings 16:8–24; Genesis 32:1–2; 2 Kings 4:8; Exodus 6:23; Ecclesiastes 7:28; Habakkuk 1:7

settings.what: Praise again and the dance (6:4–7:9; Hebrew 6:4–7:10)
settings.by: The man (6:4–9a); the queens and concubines or the chorus (6:9b–10); the woman or the man (6:11–12); the chorus (6:13a); the Shulammite or the man (6:13b); the man (7:1–9)
settings.to: The woman; the queens and the concubines; the daughters
settings.when: after the second search, when the lovers are reunited, in the poem's world
settings.why: To restate his praise at a deeper pitch: she is chosen from a world of women; she is dazzling; the crowd wants to look at her; and he answers with the fourth wasf, from her feet to her head.
settings.readers: For a wedding feast, the dance and the long praise were the high point; for a scribal school, a model of the descriptive song; for the temple community, a picture of God's chosen people.
views: Wetzstein's bride dance and its praise song (Delitzsch).
The unit begins a new section after the second search (Murphy).
God's praise of his chosen nation (Targum).

settings.what: 'Who is this who looks down like the dawn?'
settings.by: Debated: the queens and concubines of 6:9; the daughters; the man
settings.to: The group that has just praised her
settings.when: as she appears in the poem's world
settings.why: A question of amazement that leads from the praise of her as 'one' to the description of her as the sun, moon and dawn. Its speaker decides whether the praise comes from rivals who bow, from friends, or from the lover.
settings.readers: A hearer would take it as the crowd's gasp at the sight of the bride.
views: 6:9b continues into 6:10: queens and concubines praise her (Fox).
The daughters ask and the lover answers (Murphy).

settings.what: The obscure verse and the call to return
settings.by: The woman (6:12, 13b); the chorus (6:13a); the man (6:13b, debated)
settings.when: in the poem's world, after the nut garden
settings.why: 6:12 says how love swept her off her feet; 6:13 asks her to come back so they can see her, and she asks why they look. The dialogue moves the book from the garden to the dance.
settings.readers: The verses were probably already hard for the Greek translators (they read a name), so the first readers' meaning is uncertain.
views: She is carried off in a royal chariot, a motif of the bride taken to her wedding (Pope).
Her desire carries her away; the line is her surprise (Fox).
The text is corrupt and cannot be read (several scholars).

title: From the Feet Up
sum: The Shulammite is dancing, and the speaker praises her from her feet up: sandaled steps, curving thighs like the work of a master craftsman, a navel like a round bowl that never runs dry, a belly like a pile of wheat fenced with lilies, breasts like twin fawns, a neck like an ivory tower, eyes like the pools in Heshbon, a nose like a tower of Lebanon, a head like Carmel, and hair that holds a king captive. 'How beautiful you are, love, with all your delights!'

Then he says he will climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruit, and she takes up his sentence: her mouth is wine going down smoothly for her lover. The next line is hers alone: 'I belong to my lover, and his desire is toward me.' She asks him to come into the fields, to spend the night in the villages, to go early to the vineyards, and says: 'There I will give you my lovemaking.' The mandrakes smell sweet, and she has stored up fruits new and old at their doors.
readings: Read as a dance and a wedding

The Shulammite dances; the praise of her body goes upward from her feet; she then takes the lead and invites him out. The structure matches the Syrian wedding week, with its dance and its praise song (Delitzsch, Fox).
Read as the history of Israel

The Targum reads 7:1–9 as the praise of the Sanhedrin and the Temple, and 7:10–13 as Israel's return to God and her promise of devotion in the age to come, when the mandrakes (the righteous) bear fruit.
Read as Christ and the Church

The Church is the palm tree whose fruit Christ gathers on the cross (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa); her breasts are read as the two Testaments in the Latin commentaries; 7:10 is the Church's confession that she belongs to her Lord and his desire is for her.

views.H: The place names reach from Heshbon, in the east, to Damascus in the north and Carmel on the coast. The 'king' held by her hair in 7:5 may be a stock figure of royal power, bound by her as even Solomon is by the woman of 8:12. Mention of the mandrake and the vineyard points to a time between winter and spring.
views.L: The wasf from the feet up is rare; the nearest parallels are in Egyptian songs that praise the beloved's walk and in Arabic songs that praise a bride's dance. The call to go out to the fields echoes Greek pastoral (Theocritus) and Egyptian songs where lovers meet among plants.
views.J: The rabbis, followed by Rashi, read 7:1–9 as the praise of Israel's leaders and 7:10 as Israel's pledge to God. The dance of the two camps was read as Israel dancing with the angels at the giving of the Law. 'There I will give you my lovemaking' was heard as Israel offering the Temple service (the Targum), and the mandrakes as the righteous who give a good scent.
views.X: Origen and Ambrose read the palm tree as the cross; Gregory of Nyssa, the soul climbing toward God. The Marian tradition applies 7:5 ('your head like Carmel') and 7:1 to Mary. Protestant interpreters from the Puritans on read 7:10 as the believer's assurance: 'I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me'.
views.M: The woman's speech turns the praise around: where the man says 'I will climb', she says 'I belong', and then 'there I will give'. 7:10 is the Song's reversal of Genesis 3:16 (Trible). Her initiative in 7:11–13 is the most open invitation in the book. Some readers ask whether the long wasf of her body (7:1–9) puts her in the position of display.

deep.b: The wasf of 7:1–9, the fourth in the Song, differs from the others (4:1–7; 5:10–16; 6:4–10) in direction (feet to head) and in the use of images of towers, pools and mountains, large things with a touch of royal splendor: Heshbon, Lebanon, Carmel, Damascus. Some of these images describe the shape of landscape, as the Song so often does, and some the mood. Its ending is a wish and not a picture: 'may your breasts be like clusters of the vine'. Unlike 4:1–7, it ends on a speech by the woman.

Genesis 3:16 and 4:7 are the only places outside the Song that use teshuqah, 'desire'. In Genesis 3:16 the woman's desire is for her husband and he will rule over her. In 4:7 sin's desire is for Cain. The Song uses the word of the man's desire for the woman, and says no word of rule. For Trible this undoes the curse. Others think the echo is too thin to build on and that the Song is simply a poem of mutual love, not a commentary on Genesis. Both agree that the Song shows a love between equals, in which each says 'I belong to you'. Notes at 2:16 and 6:3 show how the formula of belonging changes.

deep.title: Why the wasf runs upward
deep.b: The wasf of 4:1–7 runs from the head down, and 7:1–9 from the feet up. I suggest the direction follows what the eye can do: in 4:1–7 the bride stands still behind her veil and he looks down from her face; in 7:1–9 she is dancing, and the eye starts with her moving feet and climbs. If so, the direction is not an accident but a way of showing where she is looking from. I have not found this proposed; Fox notes that the two lists differ, and the dance in 6:13 is widely discussed, but the link between the dance and the upward order is my own guess.
deep.refs: Song of Songs 4:1–7; Song of Songs 6:13; Song of Songs 7:1–9

echoes: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 4:7; Genesis 30:14–16; Ruth 3:7; Numbers 21:25–30; Isaiah 15:4; Judges 4:5; Ezekiel 16:4; Proverbs 9:2

settings.what: The praise from the feet up (Hebrew 7:2–10)
settings.by: The man (or the chorus, 7:1–5); the man (7:6–8); the woman (7:9b)
settings.when: in the dance of the two camps, in the poem's world
settings.why: To praise her in motion: the eye follows her up from the feet; he says what he wants (to climb the palm tree); she takes the sentence and answers.
settings.readers: A wedding crowd watching a dance; a school reading a model of the wasf.
views: The wasf is sung as she dances (Delitzsch).
Some scholars begin a new poem at 6:13 or at 7:1.
The Targum's praise of Israel's leaders and Temple.

settings.what: 'I belong to my lover': the fields, the vineyard and the wish (7:10–8:4; Hebrew 7:11–8:4)
settings.by: The woman
settings.to: Her lover; the daughters of Jerusalem (8:4)
settings.when: in the poem's world, after the dance; spring, at the vineyards
settings.why: To state what is true at the end of the praise (I belong to him and he wants me), to take the lead (come out to the fields), and to wish that they could kiss in public without scorn. The oath at 8:4 closes the third cycle of the book.
settings.readers: In a wedding feast this speech would be the bride's answer; for readers in a school, a model of a woman's voice.
views: The woman speaks as bride (Delitzsch, Garrett).
A new poem begins at 7:10 or 7:11 (Fox, Murphy).
Israel promises love to God in the age to come (Targum).

settings.what: 'His desire is toward me'
settings.by: The woman
settings.when: after the dance
settings.why: The woman sums up her place: belonging to him, and wanted by him. The wording recalls Genesis 3:16 and 4:7.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the Eden story would hear the line as an answer to the curse.
views: Other scholars think the echo is too slight to build on; the Song is a poem of mutual love, not a commentary on Genesis.

traditions.q: Is sexual desire in marriage good in itself, and what does the Song say to the unmarried?
views: Marital love is a gift of God, and the acts by which the spouses become one are 'noble and honorable' (Catechism 2362); sex is ordered both to the spouses' union and to children. Pope John Paul II's lectures on the 'theology of the body' read the Song as a poem of mutual self-giving. Virginity for the Kingdom and marriage both come from the Lord (Catechism 1618–1620), and chastity is asked of the engaged and the unmarried (Catechism 2348–2350).

Marriage is a sacrament, crowned in the liturgy; married life and monastic life are both blessed paths, and the Song's main reading in the Church is of the soul's love for Christ, with married love as its earthly sign. Monks and nuns read the Song as their own prayer.

Luther praised marriage as God's order and the best life for most people (The Estate of Marriage, 1522), and rejected monastic vows as a ground of merit. His lectures on the Song read it as Solomon's praise of good government; later Lutherans read it also as Christ and the Church and as married love.
Anabaptist confessions treat marriage as a covenant between one man and one woman within the believing community and honor singleness as well.
Pentecostal teachers generally speak as most evangelicals do: the Song celebrates married love, and sex belongs inside marriage. Teaching varies from one body to another.

The Song is read widely as God's celebration of married sex, a book that tells husbands and wives that desire is good and the bed is blessed. Many teachers use the oath of 2:7 in teaching on waiting until marriage. Some warn against reading the Song only as a manual.

title: Strong as Death
sum: The woman wishes her lover were her brother, so she could kiss him in the street without anyone looking down on her, and take him to her mother's house. She repeats the embrace of 2:6 and the oath for the third time: do not wake love until it wants to. Then comes a question, 'Who is this climbing up from the wilderness, leaning on her lover?' and a line about an apple tree and a mother in labor. She asks him to set her like a seal on his heart, because love is as strong as death, jealousy as hard as Sheol, and its sparks are sparks of fire, a flame of Yah. Many waters cannot put it out; no wealth can buy it.

The book ends with two short scenes. Her brothers talk about their little sister, who has no breasts: if she is a wall they will build a silver battlement on her, and if a door they will bar her with cedar. She answers, 'I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers.' Solomon has a vineyard at Baal-hamon and leases it for a thousand silver pieces each; she has her own vineyard, in front of her, and he may keep his thousand. The man asks to hear her voice, and she sends him off with the book's last words: 'Hurry, my lover, and be like a gazelle on the mountains of spices.'
readings: Read as love poetry

The Song's summary of itself. Love is as strong as death; it cannot be bought; a woman is not a possession of her brothers or of a king; the lovers do not finish, but part and meet again on the hills (Fox, Exum, Garrett).
Read as the story of God and Israel

In the Targum and the midrash, 8:6–7 is Israel's love of God, tested by exile and the nations (the many waters), and 8:14 is her prayer for God to hasten the redemption. Solomon is God and the vineyard is Israel.
Read as Christ and the Church

The seal is Christ's love or the Spirit; the love strong as death is the Passion; the little sister is the Gentile Church not yet grown (Origen); the last prayer is for Christ's return (Revelation 22:20).

views.H: The poem names Baal-hamon, a place unknown, and speaks of tenants and silver. The numbers (a thousand, two hundred) suggest a literary figure; the practice of leasing a vineyard is known (Isaiah 5; Matthew 21:33). The family scene with brothers deciding a girl's future matches the practice of Genesis 24 and 34.
views.L: The last verses read like a proverb of love, a family scene and a riddle of two vineyards, then a farewell. The closing line returns to the gazelle of 2:9, 2:17: Fox sees a rounding off of the book. Egyptian love songs likewise end with the lovers apart, longing.
views.J: Rabbi Akiva called the Song the holy of holies (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5); the rabbis took 8:6–7 as Israel's love for God. The Targum retells 8:14 as Israel's prayer in exile. In the synagogue the Song is read at Passover.
views.X: For Origen and Bernard's continuers, 8:6 is the love of Christ that went to death; the flame is the Spirit's. Origen's commentary is usually cited for reading the little sister as the Church of the Gentiles. John of the Cross, in the Spiritual Canticle, and Teresa of Ávila use the Song for the soul's union with God, and his 'Living Flame of Love' echoes the language of the flame. The Puritans read the seal as assurance of salvation.
views.M: The woman answers her brothers, Solomon and her lover in her own voice and sets terms: seal me, but I am not for sale; I am a wall, not a door. Exum reads the vineyard as a woman's reclaimed freedom. Others warn that the brothers' control is not undone and that the last line leaves the couple still apart.

deep.b: These two verses (8:6–7) are the most quoted in the Song, at weddings and funerals. They are also the nearest the book comes to saying what it is about. Love is like death in that it takes a person and cannot be refused; like Sheol in that it does not let go; like fire in that it burns without being put out; and unlike anything in the world in that it cannot be bought. The comparison with death says 'as strong as', not 'stronger than'. The dark side of the passage is jealousy: the Hebrew word covers a love that will not share its beloved. The bridal imagery of the New Testament does not quote these verses, but Christian readers have heard the Passion in them from early on.

The last scene is the book's final argument. Solomon has a vineyard that he rents out for a thousand pieces of silver; the woman has her own, and it is in front of her. Everything about Solomon's vineyard is calculation: tenants, payments, shares. Hers is not for hire. Her brothers made her guard other vineyards and she did not guard her own (1:6); now she says it is hers to keep. The king whose name opens the book as its patron (1:1) is addressed by name at the end as one who may keep his thousand. Whether he is the lover, a rival, or a foil is argued in the notes and in the book's opening pages.

deep.title: A wall that 'finds peace'
deep.b: In 8:9–10 the brothers talk about a wall and a door, and she says she is a wall with towers who 'finds peace' (shalom) in his eyes. In Deuteronomy 20:10–11 a besieged city that 'answers peace' opens its gates and is spared. I suggest the verse pictures a fortified city that opens to a lover who comes with peace, not with force: a wall with towers that is not stormed but welcomes its king. This fits the pun on Shelomoh in the next verse. Some commentators note the siege language of the passage; I have not found this exact reading of 'finds peace' argued, so it is my own suggestion and I hold it loosely.

echoes: Genesis 29:11; Genesis 38:18; Exodus 20:5; Exodus 28:29; Numbers 25:11; Psalm 93:4; Isaiah 5:1–7; Isaiah 7:23; Proverbs 6:34–35; 1 Kings 11:3; 2 Corinthians 1:22; Revelation 22:20

settings.what: The seal and the flame, the little sister and the two vineyards (8:5–14)
settings.by: The woman, the man (8:13), the brothers (8:8–9, debated), unnamed voices (8:5a, 8:11–12 debated)
settings.to: Her lover; the daughters of Jerusalem (8:4); Solomon (8:12)
settings.when: in the poem's world, after the journey of the book
settings.why: To bring the book to its summary: love's strength and its price, the freedom of the woman against family and king, and the open end of the call to hurry. These verses sum up what the book has asked of its reader.
settings.readers: For a wedding, the seal and the flame would be the blessing of the couple. For a school, a closing wisdom saying. For the temple community, a word on God's love for Israel strong enough to endure exile.
views: The unit sums up the book (Fox, Garrett).
The last scenes are Israel's love, exile and prayer (Targum).

settings.what: The seal and the flame
settings.by: The woman
settings.when: after the third oath (8:4) and the question of 8:5
settings.why: A request to be near his heart and his arm, because love, like death and Sheol, cannot be stopped, bought or put out. It is the book's statement of what love is.
settings.readers: Hearers took it as a proverb about love and a vow of faithfulness.
views: Mutual love as the strongest force in life (Fox, Exum).
The flame of Yah is God's love for his people (the rabbis, the Fathers).
Love between man and woman is a sign of God's love (Catholic and Protestant marriage tradition).

settings.what: 'Who is this?' and the apple tree
settings.by: Unnamed voices (8:5a); the woman or the man (8:5b)
settings.to: The couple; then the one who is leaning
settings.when: as the couple come up from the wilderness
settings.why: The third 'Who is this?' (3:6; 6:10) asks who is climbing up, and the next lines say who woke whom under an apple tree and where a mother gave birth. Who asks, who answers and who is addressed decides what the verse says about the couple.
settings.readers: Hearers would take the question as the crowd's, and the apple tree as the place where the couple's love began.
views: The woman speaks of waking her lover under the apple tree where his mother bore him (the Masoretic pointing).
The same letters read as 'you' feminine: the man speaks, and the tree is where her mother bore her.
The chorus asks the question, and the pair answer.
The Church or the soul comes up from the wilderness, leaning on Christ.

settings.what: The little sister and the wall
settings.by: The brothers (8:8–9, most views); the woman (8:10)
settings.to: Each other, and the woman (8:10 answers them)
settings.when: in the poem's world, as the brothers plan for their sister; the woman replies
settings.why: To show the family's control over a girl's future and her reply: she is a wall, with towers, and so she has already become a woman who finds peace, without needing their battlement or their bar.
settings.readers: A hearer who knew the brothers' role in a sister's marriage (Genesis 24:50-60; 34:13-17) would feel the contest.
views: The brothers talk, the woman replies (Fox, Exum).
She reports what her brothers said of her when she was young.
The little sister is the Gentile Church, not yet grown (Origen).

settings.what: Solomon's vineyard and hers
settings.by: The woman (the usual view); or a narrator (8:11) and the woman (8:12)
settings.when: in the poem's world; as the last argument of the book
settings.why: To say that love is not for sale: Solomon may keep his rented vineyard and his thousand; her own vineyard is in her keeping.
settings.readers: A first reader who knew Solomon's wealth (1 Kings 10) and his many wives (1 Kings 11) would hear the claim as a challenge to the king.
views: She keeps herself for her lover (Exum, Trible).
She guards herself for the one she loves (Longman).
8:11 is told by a narrator or by her brothers, and the woman answers in 8:12.
Solomon may keep his thousand, while she keeps her own vineyard for him on her terms.
Solomon is God, the vineyard is Israel and the keepers are its leaders (Targum).

settings.what: The closing call
settings.by: The man (8:13); the woman (8:14)
settings.when: the end of the poem
settings.why: To end with a call and an answer: let me hear your voice, and hurry, my lover. The book closes open, like the start, with longing.
settings.readers: Hearers took the end as a leaving, a wish for a return, or a prayer.
views: The lovers part as they met, with longing (Fox).

traditions.q: Is the 'love as strong as death' and 'flame of Yah' about human love, God's love, or both?
views: Both. The Church's long tradition reads the verse of Christ's love for the Church, strong enough to die, and of the soul's love for God; since the 20th century the tradition also reads it as the vow of married love, which images Christ's love (John Paul II, Theology of the Body).
The verse is read first of Christ's love and of the soul's love for him, and married love is honored as an image of it in the wedding service.
Luther's lectures on the Song read it chiefly of God's rule over his people and, by extension, God's love for the Church; Lutheran preaching also uses the verse for married fidelity.

Puritan preachers such as Richard Sibbes read the Song as Christ's love for the believer, and the seal as the soul's assurance of that love; modern Reformed teachers also read it as a celebration of marriage.
The verse is read at weddings as a picture of covenant faithfulness in marriage and, in preaching, as the love of Christ for his people. Some warn against using it for one meaning only.

traditions.q: Does the Song speak to the unmarried, or give a place to celibacy?
views: The Song has been read by monks and nuns as the voice of the soul wedded to Christ, and virginity for the Kingdom is held in honor beside marriage (Catechism 1618–1620).
Monastics have read the Song as their own prayer, while the Church honors marriage as a sacrament. Both are paths; the Song serves each.
Luther held that most people are made for marriage and that monastic vows were not a higher state; the Song, for Lutherans, praises love inside God's order of marriage.

The Song is not usually read as a book about vowed celibacy. The wall and towers (8:9–10) and the oath (2:7) are often taught as a call to purity before marriage, and some single readers find that the Song speaks to desire and waiting.
